params.question: Pharmacodynamics is the study of what the body does to a drug, including its absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This description actually fits pharmacokinetics, not pharmacodynamics. Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME). Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (mechanism and dose-response). Anchoring this distinction early will help throughout the course.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement describes pharmacokinetics, not pharmacodynamics. Pharmacokinetics studies what the body does to the drug (ADME), while pharmacodynamics studies what the drug does to the body (mechanism of action and dose-response).

interactions.label: A nurse plans to crush a sustained-release morphine tablet to pass it through a

params.question: A nurse plans to crush a sustained-release morphine tablet to pass it through a nasogastric feeding tube. What is the most likely consequence?

answers.text: Delayed absorption due to the enteric coating

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Crushing destroys the sustained-release matrix; the problem is the opposite — rapid, not delayed, absorption.

answers.text: Rapid release of the entire dose, risking fatal respiratory depression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Crushing destroys the controlled-release matrix, dumping what was designed to release over 8–12 hours into a few minutes — a potentially lethal dose-dumping event.

answers.text: No clinically significant effect on drug delivery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Crushing a sustained-release formulation fundamentally alters its pharmacokinetics, potentially with fatal consequences.

answers.text: Conversion of morphine to an inactive metabolite inside the tube

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Morphine does not undergo significant degradation in a feeding tube; the danger lies in dose-dumping from the destroyed matrix.

overallFeedback.feedback: Crushing a sustained-release tablet destroys its controlled-release matrix, releasing the full dose in minutes instead of hours. This is called dose-dumping and can cause fatal respiratory depression with opioids like morphine.
Exactly right. Crushing a sustained-release formulation causes dose-dumping — the entire 8–12-hour dose is released at once, risking fatal respiratory depression.

interactions.label: A patient on phenytoin has plasma levels at the upper end of the therapeutic ran

params.question: A patient on phenytoin has plasma levels at the upper end of the therapeutic range. The clinician increases the dose by 10%. What is the most likely outcome, and why?

answers.text: Levels rise proportionally by 10%, because phenytoin follows first-order kinetics at all doses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Near the therapeutic range, phenytoin's metabolising enzymes become saturated, so it shifts from first-order to zero-order kinetics — the proportional relationship breaks down.

answers.text: Levels rise disproportionately into the toxic range, because metabolic enzymes are saturated

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. At near-therapeutic concentrations, phenytoin saturates hepatic enzymes (zero-order kinetics). A constant amount — not a constant fraction — is eliminated, so even a small dose increase produces a large, non-linear rise in plasma levels.

answers.text: Levels fall because enzyme induction increases phenytoin's own metabolism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While phenytoin is an enzyme inducer, the immediate concern at the therapeutic ceiling is enzyme saturation, not induction. Saturation means a small dose increase causes a disproportionate rise.

answers.text: Levels remain unchanged because renal excretion compensates fully

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phenytoin is primarily hepatically metabolised; renal excretion plays a minor role and cannot compensate for saturated enzymes.

overallFeedback.feedback: When phenytoin's metabolising enzymes are saturated, elimination switches from first-order (constant fraction) to zero-order (constant amount per unit time). A small dose increase then causes a disproportionately large rise in plasma concentration, producing toxic effects like nystagmus and ataxia.

Well done. Near the therapeutic range, phenytoin saturates hepatic CYP2C9, shifting to zero-order kinetics — a constant amount is eliminated per unit time, so even a small dose increase causes a disproportionate rise into the toxic range (nystagmus, ataxia).

interactions.label: In opioid overdose, naloxone rapidly reverses respiratory depression by competin

params.question: In opioid overdose, naloxone rapidly reverses respiratory depression by competing with morphine at mu-opioid receptors. Which type of antagonism does this best illustrate?

answers.text: Chemical antagonism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Chemical antagonism involves direct neutralisation of a drug molecule (e.g., protamine binding heparin), not competition at a receptor binding site.

answers.text: Physiological antagonism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Physiological antagonism involves two drugs acting on entirely different receptors or pathways with opposing effects (e.g., adrenaline countering histamine in anaphylaxis). Naloxone acts at the same receptor as morphine.

answers.text: Pharmacological antagonism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Naloxone competes with morphine at the same mu-opioid receptor, displacing it and reversing its effects — the classic example of pharmacological (competitive) antagonism.

answers.text: Non-competitive antagonism

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Non-competitive antagonism involves binding at a different site on the receptor to reduce maximal response. Naloxone competes at the same orthosteric binding site as morphine, making this competitive pharmacological antagonism.

overallFeedback.feedback: Naloxone and morphine both act at the mu-opioid receptor — naloxone competes for the same binding site, displacing morphine. This is pharmacological antagonism, distinct from chemical antagonism (direct drug neutralisation) and physiological antagonism (opposing effects via different pathways).

Exactly. Pharmacological antagonism occurs when two drugs compete at the same receptor. Naloxone displaces morphine from the mu-opioid receptor, reversing respiratory depression — a life-saving application of competitive antagonism.

interactions.label: A patient develops anaphylaxis within minutes of receiving penicillin — a Type B

params.question: A patient develops anaphylaxis within minutes of receiving penicillin — a Type B adverse drug reaction. What is the correct management principle for this ADR type?

answers.text: Reduce the penicillin dose and continue therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Dose reduction is appropriate for Type A (augmented) reactions, which are dose-dependent and predictable. Type B reactions are idiosyncratic and not dose-related, so dose reduction does not help.

answers.text: Switch to another penicillin derivative with a different formulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type B reactions are often immune-mediated and related to the drug's core chemical structure. Cross-reactivity within the penicillin class makes switching within the same class inappropriate.

answers.text: Withdraw penicillin permanently and never rechallenge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Type B (bizarre/idiosyncratic) reactions demand complete, permanent withdrawal. Rechallenge risks a more severe reaction because of immunological memory.

answers.text: Add a corticosteroid and continue penicillin at the same dose

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While corticosteroids are part of anaphylaxis emergency management, continuing the offending drug is dangerous. Type B reactions require permanent withdrawal of the causative agent.

overallFeedback.feedback: Type B (bizarre/idiosyncratic) ADRs are unpredictable and not dose-dependent. Unlike Type A reactions — which can often be managed by reducing the dose — Type B reactions require complete and permanent withdrawal of the offending drug, with no rechallenge.

Well done. Type B ADRs are unpredictable, often immune-mediated, and not dose-dependent — the drug must be permanently withdrawn. This is fundamentally different from Type A reactions, where dose adjustment is often sufficient.

interactions.label: A patient on warfarin is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. Two weeks later

params.question: A patient on warfarin is started on rifampicin for tuberculosis. Two weeks later, the patient suffers an ischaemic stroke because warfarin plasma levels have dropped below the therapeutic range. Which category of drug interaction is responsible?

answers.text: Pharmaceutical interaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pharmaceutical interactions are physical or chemical incompatibilities that occur before drugs enter the body (e.g., precipitation when two drugs are mixed in the same IV line). Here, the interaction occurs inside the body.

answers.text: Pharmacodynamic interaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pharmacodynamic interactions alter a drug's effect at the receptor level without changing its plasma concentration. In this case, warfarin's blood level itself dropped due to increased metabolism.

answers.text: Pharmacokinetic interaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Rifampicin induces hepatic CYP enzymes, accelerating warfarin's metabolism and reducing its plasma concentration — a pharmacokinetic interaction at the level of drug metabolism.

answers.text: Idiosyncratic interaction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 'Idiosyncratic interaction' is not a standard category. This interaction is entirely predictable and mechanism-based: rifampicin induces the enzymes that metabolise warfarin, lowering its levels.

overallFeedback.feedback: Rifampicin is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP enzymes, which accelerates warfarin's metabolism and lowers its plasma concentration below the therapeutic range. This is a pharmacokinetic interaction — the drug's blood level is altered through changes in metabolism, not through any effect at the receptor.

Exactly right. Rifampicin induces hepatic CYP enzymes, increasing warfarin's metabolism and lowering its plasma concentration — a pharmacokinetic interaction. This is why prescribers must review all enzyme-metabolised medicines before starting rifampicin, especially narrow-therapeutic-index drugs like warfarin.
